# (PART) Knowledge graphs {-}

# Knowledge graphs and IRT {#knowledge-graphs}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* describe what a test measures as a **knowledge graph** of concepts,
  prerequisites and items, and build one with `mv_kg_build()` or
  `as_mv_kg()`;
* check a graph for problems with `mv_kg_check()` and draw it with
  `gg_kg()`;
* read a graph's **Q-matrix** and list the mastery patterns its
  **attribute hierarchy** allows;
* turn a graph into a confirmatory multidimensional IRT model with
  `mv_kg_model()` and `mv_kg_irt()`, and test the graph's claims against
  simpler and stricter models;
* check a graph against data with `mv_kg_fit()` and explain item
  difficulty with it using `mv_kg_explain()`.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[Knowledge graph](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#knowledge-graph),
[Q-matrix](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#q-matrix),
[attribute hierarchy](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#attribute-hierarchy),
[multidimensional IRT](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#multidimensional-irt),
[likelihood-ratio test](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#likelihood-ratio-test).

## The ideas

Every test is built on claims about what it measures. A blueprint says
which content each item covers; a curriculum says that some ideas must be
learned before others; a teacher knows that an item about subtracting
mixed numbers also needs borrowing. Most of these claims stay in documents
and heads. A **knowledge graph** writes them down in a form a computer can
check and a model can use. It has three kinds of parts.

* **Concepts** (also called skills, attributes or objectives): What the
  test is meant to tell us about.
* **Relations between concepts.** The most useful is **prerequisite of**:
  Equivalent fractions before adding fractions with unlike denominators.
  Prerequisite edges point forward in the learning order and should never
  form a cycle. A weaker relation, **related to**, links concepts where
  neither comes first.
* **Items**, each linked to the concepts it **measures**. These links are
  the rows of the **Q-matrix** [@tatsuoka1984]: One row per item, one
  column per concept, with a 1 where the item needs the concept.

The graph connects two traditions in psychometrics. In **multidimensional
IRT**, the Q-matrix is the loading pattern of a confirmatory model: Each
concept is a factor, and an item has a slope only on the concepts it
measures (Chapter \@ref(dimensionality)). In **cognitive diagnosis**, the
same Q-matrix says which skills an item needs, and prerequisite edges form
an **attribute hierarchy** [@leighton2004; @templin2014]: A student can
master a concept only after mastering its prerequisites, so some mastery
patterns are impossible. Knowledge space theory [@doignon1999] builds a
whole theory of assessment on such structures.

A graph is a set of claims, and each claim can be wrong. An item can be
linked to the wrong concept, a prerequisite can be missing or reversed,
and two concepts can be impossible to tell apart because the same items
measure them. The work in this chapter is to make the claims explicit,
check what can be checked without data, and then let the data speak.

## Example 1: A graph for fraction subtraction

Tatsuoka's fraction subtraction data are the best-known real data in
cognitive diagnosis: 536 middle school students answered 20 items such as
$4\frac{1}{3} - 2\frac{4}{3}$, and the items were coded on eight
attributes [@tatsuoka2002; @decarlo2011; @delatorre2004]. mirtverse
stores the responses as `fraction_subtraction` and the Q-matrix as a
knowledge graph, `fraction_subtraction_kg`.

```{r data-knowledge-graphs-1}
resp <- fraction_subtraction
kg <- fraction_subtraction_kg
```

```{r}
kg
tidy(kg)
```

The graph has eight concepts and 20 items, with 56 item-to-concept links.
No prerequisite edges were published with the Q-matrix, so the graph has
none yet. `tidy()` counts the items linked to each concept (`links`).
`subtract_numerators` is needed by 19 of the 20 items, while
`column_borrow` is needed by only two. Before any data are used,
`mv_kg_check()` looks for problems in the structure itself.

```{r}
mv_kg_check(kg)
```

The check finds one thing to review: Two items are too few to estimate
`column_borrow` as its own dimension. A concept that nearly every item
needs, like `subtract_numerators`, has the opposite problem: It is hard to
separate from overall proficiency. Neither is an error in the graph, but
both limit what a model can learn about these concepts.

```{r kg-fs, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "The fraction subtraction graph: Eight attributes on the left, each joined to the items that need it."}
gg_kg(kg)
```

Now suppose a mathematics teacher states two prerequisites as hypotheses:
Borrowing from the whole number needs the whole number to be separated
from the fraction first, and column borrowing needs subtracting numerators.
We add these edges to the same concepts and items.

```{r}
concepts <- tidy(kg)
concepts <- concepts[concepts$kind == "concept", ]
kg_h <- mv_kg_build(
  concepts = data.frame(concept = concepts$node, label = concepts$label),
  edges = data.frame(from = c("separate_whole", "subtract_numerators"),
                     to = c("borrow_whole", "column_borrow")),
  items = mv_kg_qmatrix(kg),
  name = "Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites")
kg_h
```

The print-out now gives a learning order. The hierarchy has a practical
consequence: With eight concepts there are $2^8 = 256$ possible mastery
patterns, and each prerequisite rules out the patterns where a concept is
mastered without its prerequisite.

```{r}
patterns <- mv_kg_hierarchy(kg_h)
nrow(patterns)
attr(patterns, "possible")
```

Two edges remove 112 of the 256 patterns. A diagnostic model that respects
the hierarchy has fewer classes to estimate, and the hierarchy itself can
be tested by comparing models with and without it.

## Example 2: From graph to IRT model

`mv_kg_model()` writes the confirmatory mirt model a graph implies, and
`mv_kg_irt()` fits it. Eight correlated dimensions on 536 students is a
large model that takes many minutes to fit, so we work with a smaller
graph: The three concepts with the clearest roles, separating the whole
number, borrowing, and finding a common denominator. `mv_kg_subset()` keeps
these concepts, the prerequisite between two of them, and the 16 items that
need at least one of them.

```{r}
kg3 <- mv_kg_subset(kg_h, c("separate_whole", "borrow_whole", "common_denominator"))
kg3
q <- mv_kg_qmatrix(kg3)
resp3 <- resp[rownames(q)]
spec <- mv_kg_model(kg3)
cat(attr(spec, "item_syntax"))
```

Each concept is a factor, and each item loads on the concepts its row of
the Q-matrix names; items that need two concepts load on both. By default
all concepts correlate. The `structure` argument changes that:
`structure = "graph"` lets only concepts joined by an edge correlate, a
strict reading of the graph in which concepts without an edge are
unrelated.

```{r}
m_uni <- mirt(resp3, 1, verbose = FALSE)
m_graph <- mv_kg_irt(kg3, resp3)
m_strict <- mv_kg_irt(kg3, resp3, structure = "graph")
anova(m_uni, m_graph)
anova(m_strict, m_graph)
```

Two comparisons answer two questions. Against a single dimension, the
three-concept model fits far better: The likelihood-ratio statistic is
about 394 on 13 degrees of freedom, and BIC drops by more than 300. The
items measure more than one proficiency, in the way the graph describes.
Against the strict model, the correlated model also wins clearly: Finding a
common denominator has no edge in the graph, yet it correlates with the
other two concepts.

```{r}
round(summary(m_graph, verbose = FALSE)$fcor, 2)
```

Separating the whole number and finding a common denominator correlate at
about 0.77, much more than the two concepts the teacher linked (about
0.37). This is a typical finding, not a failure: A prerequisite edge says
something about the *order* of learning, and concepts that are learned in
the same lessons correlate whether or not one is a prerequisite of the
other. The correlations are a reason to look again at the graph, for
example to ask whether a related-to edge is missing.

The fitted model is an ordinary mirt model, so everything from the earlier
chapters works on it, and the graph travels with it.

```{r}
pars <- tidy(m_graph)
head(pars[pars$estimate != 0, ])
attr(m_graph, "mv_kg")
```

`as_mv_kg()` also goes the other way: Given any confirmatory mirt model, it
reads the loading pattern back into a graph, which is a quick way to draw a
model you already have.

## Example 3: Checking the graph against data

The comparisons above test the graph as a whole. `mv_kg_fit()` looks for
the places where the data disagree with it. For each item, it asks whether
the item agrees more with another concept than with its own: It correlates
the item with the rest score of every concept, corrected for how reliable
each rest score is. For each pair of concepts, it turns the factor
correlations of the correlated model into **partial correlations**, the
correlation of two concepts once the others are held constant. Concepts
that are directly related keep a clear partial correlation; concepts
related only through others do not. We can pass in the model we already
have.

```{r}
check <- mv_kg_fit(kg3, resp3, model = m_graph)
check
tidy(check, "relations")
```

No item is flagged: Every item agrees best with a concept it is linked
to. The relation evidence makes the earlier observation precise. Holding
borrowing constant, separating the whole number and finding a common
denominator still have a partial correlation of about 0.73, while the
teacher's prerequisite (separate_whole -> borrow_whole) drops to about
0.14. Because the two concepts' items are about equally hard, the
suggestion is a related edge rather than a prerequisite.

```{r kg-fit-fs, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "The evidence on the three-concept graph: Partial correlations next to each pair, and the suggested related edge as a dashed line."}
gg_kg_fit(check, items = "all")
```

`mv_kg_refine()` would add the edge. Whether to do so is a content
question: Both skills come up when students handle mixed numbers with
unlike denominators, so a related edge is plausible, but the data alone
cannot say why the concepts go together.

A graph also makes claims about difficulty. `mv_kg_explain()` fits an
explanatory Rasch model with the eirm package [@bulut2021] in which
the graph predicts each item's difficulty: One difficulty per concept (a
linear logistic test model, with a random item effect for what the
concepts leave unexplained), or the item's depth in the learning order.

```{r}
explain <- mv_kg_explain(kg, resp)
explain
```

The eight attributes explain most of the differences in item difficulty.
Borrowing from the whole number and converting a whole number to a
fraction add the most difficulty, and subtracting numerators, which almost
every item needs, the least. The teacher's two prerequisites, in
contrast, say little about difficulty:

```{r}
mv_kg_explain(kg_h, resp, predictors = "depth")
```

Items that need more attributes are harder, but once that is taken into
account, an item's depth in the teacher's learning order adds little. A
prerequisite that does not show up as a difference in difficulty is not
necessarily wrong, but it is a claim the data do not support yet.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Add a third hypothesis to `kg_h`: Converting a whole number to a
   fraction (`convert_whole`) is a prerequisite of borrowing
   (`borrow_whole`). How many mastery patterns are left?
2. Add a cycle by also making `borrow_whole` a prerequisite of
   `separate_whole`. What does `mv_kg_check()` report, and what happens to
   `mv_kg_hierarchy()`?
3. Fit the three-concept model with `structure = "orthogonal"`. How does it
   compare with the correlated model, and what does that say about scoring
   the three concepts separately?
4. Draw `kg3` with `gg_kg()`, highlighting `common_denominator`. Which items
   does it share with `separate_whole`?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. a third prerequisite
edges3 <- data.frame(from = c("separate_whole", "subtract_numerators", "convert_whole"),
                     to = c("borrow_whole", "column_borrow", "borrow_whole"))
kg_h3 <- mv_kg_build(data.frame(concept = concepts$node, label = concepts$label),
                     edges = edges3, items = mv_kg_qmatrix(kg))
nrow(mv_kg_hierarchy(kg_h3))

# 2. a cycle
kg_cyc <- mv_kg_build(data.frame(concept = concepts$node),
                      edges = rbind(edges3, data.frame(from = "borrow_whole",
                                                       to = "separate_whole")),
                      items = mv_kg_qmatrix(kg))
mv_kg_check(kg_cyc)
try(mv_kg_hierarchy(kg_cyc))

# 3. uncorrelated concepts
m_orth <- mv_kg_irt(kg3, resp3, structure = "orthogonal")
anova(m_orth, m_graph)

# 4. shared items
gg_kg(kg3, highlight = "common_denominator")
q[q[, "common_denominator"] == 1 & q[, "separate_whole"] == 1, ]
```

1. Borrowing now needs both separating and converting, so more patterns are
   ruled out: 120 of the 256 remain.
2. The check reports a `cycle` block flag: Separating the whole number
   would have to come both before and after borrowing, so no learning order
   exists. `mv_kg_hierarchy()` stops with an error, because a cycle allows
   no consistent set of patterns.
3. The orthogonal model fits much worse than the correlated one (the
   likelihood-ratio statistic is about 277 on 3 degrees of freedom). The
   concepts share a lot of variance, so three separate scores would repeat
   much of the same information; reporting them separately needs care
   (Chapter \@ref(reporting)).
4. Two items, FS05 and FS13, need both concepts; FS13 also needs
   borrowing. The other common denominator items (FS01 to FS03) involve no
   whole numbers. Items that load on two concepts help the model separate
   the concepts from their correlation.

</details>

## In the lab {-}

<div class="lab">
**Lab 11, Repairing a knowledge graph** (`run_lab("kg-repair")`): A
district's curriculum team has written a knowledge graph for its Grade 5
fractions test, and diagnostic reports will follow it. Check the graph
against the students' answers with `mv_kg_fit()`, find an item linked to
the wrong concept and a missing prerequisite, repair the graph with
`mv_kg_refine()`, and show what the repair changes.
</div>

## Further reading {-}

Tatsuoka [-@tatsuoka1984] introduced the Q-matrix with the fraction
subtraction data; DeCarlo [-@decarlo2011] and de la Torre and Douglas
[-@delatorre2004] reanalysed them with diagnostic models. Leighton, Gierl
and Hunka [-@leighton2004] describe the attribute hierarchy method, and
Templin and Bradshaw [-@templin2014] show how to test hierarchies with
diagnostic classification models. Doignon and Falmagne [-@doignon1999]
develop knowledge space theory, the mathematical theory of prerequisite
structures in assessment.
